title: 7.3.20 Unit 5 Check: classes, objects and methods
description: Eight multiple-choice questions closing Unit 5: class versus instance, the constructor, this, method syntax, separate state on two instances, arrays of instances, where a variable lives, and what a class variable is. Checked instantly.

questions.question: You call `new Sprite(100, 100, 40, 40)` three times. What do you have afterwards?
options: One sprite that has been moved twice
Three sprites, each with its own position and size
One sprite and two errors, because a class can only be used once
Three variables, but only the last one is usable
questions.explanation: `new` runs the constructor and hands back a fresh instance every time. Three calls, three objects — which is why you store them in three variables or in an array.

questions.question: What is a constructor for?
options: It destroys the object when it is no longer needed
It runs once per frame to draw the object
It runs once, when the object is created, and sets up its starting state
It is another name for `draw()`
questions.explanation: The constructor runs exactly once, at `new`. That is where a new object's properties get their first values: `this.hp = 10`, `this.sprite = new Sprite(...)`.

questions.question: Inside `enemy.takeHit(1)`, what does `this` mean?
options: The class `Enemy`
The number 1
The specific enemy the method was called on
The file, so `this` is the same everywhere
questions.explanation: `this` is the object before the dot. Call `otherEnemy.takeHit(1)` and the same method body runs with `this` set to `otherEnemy`, so it changes that enemy's health instead.

questions.question: Which line declares a method correctly inside a class body?
options: `function tick() { this.n += 1; }`
`tick() { this.n += 1; }`
`method tick() { this.n += 1; }`
`let tick = () => { this.n += 1; };`
questions.explanation: Inside a class body you drop the `function` keyword: a method is `name(params) { ... }`. Writing `function tick()` there is a syntax error, and the file will not run at all.

questions.question: Two enemies are built with `new Enemy(100, 100)`. You put one of them through `takeHit(3)`. What is the other one's health?
options: Three lower, because they share the same `hp`
Zero, because `takeHit` resets every enemy
Unchanged, because each instance keeps its own copy of `hp`
`undefined`, because properties are cleared after a method runs
questions.explanation: `hp` is an instance property: each object got its own copy when its constructor ran. Changing one instance's `this.hp` cannot reach the other, which is the whole reason to use objects instead of shared variables.

questions.question: You have `enemies`, an array of `Enemy` instances. What does a loop over it give you that three named variables did not?
options: It makes each enemy run faster
It lets one method call reach every enemy, however many there are
It stops the enemies from sharing properties
It is required before `filter` can be used on them
questions.explanation: A loop turns "do this to each enemy" into one line, no matter whether there are three or thirty. That is what makes a spawner possible: the array grows, and the loop keeps working.

questions.question: A method declares `let step = 3;` and uses it. What happens on the next call to the same method?
options: `step` is still 3, and any changes made to it are still there
`step` is a brand-new local, made again from the declaration
The declaration is skipped, because `step` already exists
The method errors, because a local cannot be declared twice
questions.explanation: A local lives for one call. The next call builds a fresh one from the same line, so it starts at 3 again no matter what the last call did with it. Anything that must survive belongs on `this`.

questions.question: `class Enemy { static spawned = 0; }` and two enemies exist. Which expression counts how many enemies have ever been built?
options: `enemy.spawned`, which reads one enemy's own property
`this.spawned`, written inside `draw()`
`Enemy.spawned`, which reads the property that belongs to the class
`enemy.spawned + enemy.spawned`, to add up both enemies
questions.explanation: A `static` property belongs to the class, so it is reached through the class name. `enemy.spawned` looks for a property on that one object, finds nothing, and gives `undefined`.
